article.title: Does Trump have momentum?
article.subtitle: And what does “momentum” mean in the context of an election forecast?

extraction.summary: Model Talk column noting that Trump has become the nominal favorite (50.2% vs. Harris 49.5%, with a 0.3% chance of a 269-269 tie) in the Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model, driven mostly by gains in the Blue Wall states since his Sept. 27 low of 41.7%. Silver explains that his forecasts and polling averages are explicitly designed to be 'momentumless', meaning they avoid autocorrelation. He says the polling averages are tuned to predict polls about two weeks out, with a more aggressive setting at the end of the race. He argues that momentum effects are overrated in two-way general elections. He frames Trump's recent gains partly as mean reversion toward the economic fundamentals, which imply roughly Harris +1 in the popular vote. He also discusses how non-response bias, herding and prediction-market trader behavior can create artificial momentum.

findings.statement: The Silver Bulletin election forecasts are explicitly designed to be 'momentumless'. The best prediction of what the forecast will say tomorrow is what it says today, so the forecast avoids autocorrelation and behaves like a martingale.
findings.rationale: Predictable future movement would mean the forecast is leaving information on the table.
findings.evidence_quote: The Silver Bulletin election forecasts are explicitly designed to be momentumless. In other words, the best prediction of what the forecast says tomorrow is what it says today

findings.statement: The sensitivity parameters of the Silver Bulletin polling averages were tuned with minimizing autocorrelation, both positive and negative, as one of the most important objectives.
findings.rationale: Averages that are too sensitive produce mean reversion (negative autocorrelation). Averages that are too sluggish produce positive autocorrelation, leaving predictable trend information unused.
findings.evidence_quote: one of the most important factors I sought to optimize for when tuning their parameters was minimizing autocorrelation — that is, having neither positive autocorrelation nor negative autocorrelation

findings.statement: Silver defines negative autocorrelation as an over-sensitive average whose moves predictably reverse: a candidate going from +1 to +2 implies a reversion to +1.5 next week. He defines positive autocorrelation as an over-sluggish average whose moves predictably continue: +1 to +2 implies +3 next week.

quantities.name: example margin path
quantities.context: Hypothetical Trump margin in Arizona used to illustrate autocorrelation

findings.evidence_quote: If Trump rising from +1 to +2 implies that the polling average next week will be +3, this is positive autocorrelation

findings.statement: The Silver Bulletin polling averages tend to be more sensitive to new polls than most other averages.
findings.rationale: This follows from tuning to minimize autocorrelation rather than to minimize visible volatility.
findings.evidence_quote: the Silver Bulletin polling averages tend to be more sensitive than most

findings.statement: Silver says professional model builders tend to make their models too sluggish, 'easing into' changes more than is optimal for predictive accuracy, because they fear looking silly if the forecast bounces around. Laypeople make the opposite error and overreact to new information.
findings.rationale: The reluctance to show volatility comes from reputational concerns rather than accuracy.
findings.evidence_quote: They think it makes them look silly if their forecast is bouncing around a lot, so they build models that “ease into” changes more than is optimal

findings.statement: The Silver Bulletin polling averages are designed to look two weeks out: today's average should optimally predict what new polls will say two weeks from now. This is a middle ground between a short-term focus, which calls for an aggressive average, and a 30-day focus, which calls for a conservative one.

quantities.name: prediction horizon of polling average
quantities.context: Target horizon used in tuning, except at the end of the race

findings.rationale: The best short-term prediction may extend a bounce, while the best long-term prediction may revert, because bounces from debates and conventions can be short-lived.
findings.evidence_quote: our polling averages are designed to look two weeks out — that is, the polling average today should optimally predict what new polls will say two weeks from now

findings.statement: At the end of the race, the Silver Bulletin polling averages switch to a more aggressive (more sensitive) setting, because there is no time left for reversion to the mean.
findings.rationale: Near election day, the short-term and final-outcome horizons converge.
findings.evidence_quote: except at the end of the race when there’s no time left for reversion to the mean, and we use a more aggressive setting

findings.statement: Because the Silver Bulletin averages are tuned for a two-week horizon, they may understate momentum over the very short term.
findings.evidence_quote: It’s possible we’ll understate momentum over the very short term, however.

findings.statement: Bounces from events such as debates and conventions can be short-lived. A post-debate gain may keep growing for about a week but revert within about 30 days.

quantities.name: hypothetical debate example
quantities.value: 2-point lead to 3-point lead; next week 4; in 30 days back to 2
quantities.context: Illustration of how short-run and medium-run predictions can differ

findings.rationale: Favorable media coverage and viral clips can extend a bounce in the short run before it fades.
findings.evidence_quote: bounces from events like debates and conventions can be short-lived

findings.statement: As an empirical matter, polling averages more closely resemble random walks than trend-continuing (momentum) processes, at least over the medium term. Silver first concluded this in a 2010 analysis.
findings.rationale: The behavior is analogous to efficient markets.
findings.evidence_quote: polling generally does not show this pattern, at least not over the medium term. Instead, as an empirical matter, polling averages more closely resemble random walks.

findings.statement: Outside of major events like debates, the Silver Bulletin presidential model typically does not move very much from day to day.
findings.evidence_quote: Outside of major events like debates, the model typically does not move very much from day to day.

findings.statement: As of Oct. 17, 2024, the Silver Bulletin economic index implied that Harris 'should' win the national popular vote by roughly 1 percentage point.
findings.evidence_quote: our current economic index implies that Harris “should” win the popular vote by roughly 1 percentage point

findings.statement: The Silver Bulletin models include a 'fundamentals' component based on factors like the economy and incumbency. Its weight is phased out over the course of the campaign, and by mid-October it gets little weight.
findings.evidence_quote: the fundamentals do not currently get very much weight in our forecast — they are phased out over the course of the campaign

findings.statement: Polling moves toward the fundamentals baseline can be read as mean reversion rather than momentum. Silver views Trump's October 2024 gains as the race returning to a fundamentals-implied baseline after Harris's strong debate, which had inflated her national lead to 3-3.5 points.
findings.evidence_quote: Trump’s recent gains in the polls are actually not “momentum” but mean reversion, the race returning to its natural baseline after Harris’s strong debate

findings.statement: Fox News polling has no history of GOP bias, so a Fox News poll showing Trump ahead was treated as a high-quality signal that moved the Silver Bulletin forecast.
findings.evidence_quote: yes, it’s from Fox News, but Fox News polling has no history of GOP bias

findings.statement: Partisan non-response bias can create artificial momentum: voters may be more likely to respond to polls when their candidate is getting favorable news coverage.
findings.evidence_quote: voters may be more likely to respond to polls when their candidate is getting favorable news coverage

findings.statement: Pollster herding can create artificial momentum. Mediocre pollsters may publish more favorable numbers for a candidate who is perceived to be on an upswing, or tinker with their turnout model until results match the perceived narrative.

quantities.name: example
quantities.context: Hypothetical Pennsylvania result depending on the perceived narrative

findings.rationale: What matters in the end is votes, not polls.
findings.evidence_quote: mediocre pollsters may decide it’s safe to publish more favorable numbers for a candidate when he’s in the midst of a favorable news cycle

findings.statement: Silver says prediction markets can overstate the importance of momentum. Some traders buy shares based on reading or influencing trader sentiment rather than on changes in fundamental value, such as strong polls. Markets can also be moved by 'whales', well-bankrolled bettors who buy many contracts.
findings.rationale: Herd behavior seen in traditional and crypto assets also occurs among political prediction-market traders.
findings.evidence_quote: prediction markets are probably going too far in this case and can overstate the importance of momentum

findings.statement: In mid-October 2024, the Silver Bulletin model showed a trend toward Trump slightly more explicitly than other models did, matching the direction of prediction markets.
findings.rationale: This is consistent with the Silver Bulletin averages being more sensitive than most.
findings.evidence_quote: the Silver Bulletin model has been slightly more explicit about showing a trend toward Trump over the past week or so than other models

findings.statement: Silver says there is no special significance to the 50% threshold. A move from 49.4% to 50.2% matters no more than one from 43.1% to 43.9%, and people should not treat a 51/49 forecast very differently from a 49/51 forecast.
findings.evidence_quote: there’s no special significance to the 50-yard line

findings.statement: The Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model reports an explicit probability of a 269-269 Electoral College tie, separate from each candidate's win probability. On Oct. 17, 2024 the figures were Trump 50.2%, Harris 49.5% and tie 0.3%.
findings.evidence_quote: There’s also a 0.3 percent chance of a 269-269 Electoral College tie.

findings.statement: Between Sept. 27 and Oct. 17, 2024, Trump's win probabilities in the Silver Bulletin model rose most in the Blue Wall states (MI +12.6, WI +8.9, PA +8.7 points). Gains elsewhere were incremental (GA +4.6, NV +3.5, NC about +3, AZ about +2.6), while the national probability rose +8.5 points. This shows correlated, regionally clustered movement.

The Silver Bulletin model computes tipping-point probabilities by state. On Oct. 17, 2024, the Blue Wall states (MI, WI, PA) had a combined 61% chance of being the tipping-point state, and North Carolina had surpassed Wisconsin in tipping-point odds.
findings.evidence_quote: the Blue Wall states have a combined 61 percent chance of being the tipping-point state

findings.statement: Trump's lowest win probability in the Silver Bulletin model was 41.7% on Sept. 27, 2024, about two weeks after the debate. From then to Oct. 17 his odds rose day-over-day 12 times, fell 7 times and were unchanged once. The nominal favorite had changed four times during the cycle.
findings.rationale: Silver wants to avoid ignoring a slow, incremental trend.
findings.evidence_quote: his odds have improved day-over-day 12 times, decreased 7 times, and been unchanged once

findings.statement: The Silver Bulletin forecast-history chart shows Trump at about 62% at model launch in late July 2024, Harris overtaking him in early August, Trump peaking around 64% near Sept. 8 before the debate, a drop after the Sept. 10 debate, and convergence near 50/50 by Oct. 17. Kennedy's probability shows at roughly 0% until he dropped out in late August.

political_insights.insight: Bandwagon and momentum effects are overrated in two-way general elections because media sentiment shifts rapidly. A 'candidate rising' storyline becomes stale after about two weeks, and the media then looks for a comeback narrative.
political_insights.evidence: Silver's experience as a model builder and observer of news cycles.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Do not extrapolate trends in general-election polling averages; treat them as close to a random walk.

political_insights.insight: Momentum effects can matter a great deal in multi-candidate primaries where voters behave tactically.
political_insights.evidence: In 2020, as Elizabeth Warren slumped in the polls, many of her voters switched to Bernie Sanders as the more viable progressive alternative to Joe Biden.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Primary models may need dynamics that allow trends to continue, unlike general-election models.

political_insights.insight: Republicans more actively cultivate momentum narratives and develop a pack mentality after strong Trump polls, while Democrats tend to fear that leads will evaporate.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Expect prediction markets and partisan commentary to overreact to pro-Trump trends.

political_insights.insight: In 2024, the Blue Wall states (MI, WI, PA) dominated Harris's path to victory. North Carolina could substitute for Michigan or Wisconsin on its own, but substituting for Pennsylvania would also require winning Nevada.
political_insights.evidence: 61% combined tipping-point probability for the Blue Wall states; footnote 3.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Model state correlation regionally; Blue Wall states tend to move together.

political_insights.insight: Harris remained a clear but not overwhelming favorite in the popular vote while being roughly 50/50 in the Electoral College, which reflects a Republican Electoral College bias.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Simulate the Electoral College gap separately from the popular vote.

references.description: Silver's 2010 FiveThirtyEight article on momentum in polling, which concluded that polling averages resemble random walks
Silver Bulletin economic index used for the fundamentals
Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential forecast and its data download ('Get the data')

open_questions: The exact functional form and sensitivity parameters (e.g., decay or half-life) of the Silver Bulletin polling averages tuned to the two-week horizon.
When, and how much, the 'more aggressive setting' is applied at the end of the race.
The schedule by which fundamentals weight is phased out over the campaign, and its value in mid-October.
The components of the economic index and how incumbency enters the fundamentals.
How the autocorrelation-minimization objective was measured and optimized, including the backtest data used.
